drills.coachNote: You had a fork sitting on the board: your knight on e5 can jump into c6, grabbing Black's knight there, and from c6 it's still attacking the rook on d8 next — a knight that eats two pieces in two moves. Playing the slow a4 instead lets Black seize the initiative with ...Nxe5, and after Qxe5 Black plants a knight on e4, kicking around your position and forcing f3 just to survive — that's how a 5.4-pawn lead drops by 4.7 points almost instantly. Nxc6 was the move: after Qd6, Nxd8 completes the fork, and even after Qxd8 you're still mopping up with Qxg5. When your knight already touches two loose pieces, cash it in — don't give the other side time to untangle.
drills.threat: Black's knight on c6 and rook on d8 both sit one knight-jump away from your knight on e5.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8 — one of them falls next move. In the game, b5 ran into Nxe5, costing about 4.6 pawns of advantage.

drills.coachNote: Black wants to keep infiltrating your second rank with the queen and rook, hoping you get distracted from his real weakness: the king on g8 is nearly defenseless, with f7 held only by the rook on f8. Qg5 let Black strike first instead — Rxf2! tore into your own king's shelter, and after Qe5 Rf3 Rf1 your mating attack had evaporated, dropping you from a completely winning position to almost nothing. Rxf7 finished it: it removes the last defender, and after Qb6 Rg7+ Kh8 Rg8# is mate. When your pieces already have the enemy king trapped, calculate the forcing capture before trying anything else.

drills.coachNote: Black's g5-pawn is attacking your bishop on f4 while his king sits exposed on d7 — that's the real story, not a fancy check. Bf5+ moved your other bishop for a check that achieves nothing forcing: Black simply blocks with e6, you retreat again to d3, and the f4 bishop you never dealt with just falls to gxf4, costing you a full piece for a pawn after exf4. Nxg5 was the answer — it removes the attacker, and after fxg5 Bxg5 you're a clean pawn up with your bishop pair aimed straight at Black's stranded king. Deal with the attacked piece before reaching for a check that doesn't threaten anything.

drills.coachNote: White wants to leave the knight on d3 alone so it can hop forward to a better square while you're busy elsewhere. c5 doesn't touch that knight at all, and White proved the point: Nc3, then after your c4 push, Nf4 jumped in and kicked your bishop off e6, costing you a tempo for nothing. Bc4 was the move that actually deals with it — it attacks the knight on d3 directly, and after Re3 Bxd3 Rxd3 Rxd3 cxd3 you trade down into an ending where White's pawns are wrecked. When an enemy piece is undefended and about to improve, challenge it before making a pawn move that ignores it.

drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: White's dark-squared bishop on c1 already watches the whole c1–h6 diagonal, so g5 was never a safe landing spot. Ng5 walked your knight straight into that line — White simply played Bxg5, and when you kicked it with f6, White grabbed another pawn with Nxe5 instead of retreating, leaving you down a full piece for nothing while still having to play Be6. Nd6 was the safer path: it tucks the knight onto a solid square, and after Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 Bg6 Bf4 the position stays roughly level with nothing lost. Before sending a piece forward, always check which diagonals or files are already aimed at that square.
